title: WHY: 2025 Future Begins with Questions
lead: In a rapidly changing world of instant answers and uncertainty, the most fundamental compass we hold is 'WHY'. WHY 2025 explores new directions and the purpose of design leadership through essential questions.

blocks.text: Our Beginnings: The Shift from 'What & How' to 'Why'

In a rapidly changing world of instant answers and uncertainty, the most fundamental compass we hold is 'WHY'. WHY 2025 explores new directions and the purpose of design leadership through essential questions.

We have grown by continuously reflecting on what we create and how we advance. Every step of our journey has held its own meaning and value, leading us to where we stand today. Today, the world seeks not only what we create and how we create it, but crucially the 'WHY' behind it all.

title: Professor Cathy Lee Moderates Future Culture Sessions at FRAME 2025
lead:
Professor Cathy Lee of Hongik University’s International Design School for Advanced
Studies (IDAS) moderated two sessions in the “Future Culture” track at FRAME 2025. The
event took place on 23 and 24 September 2025 at Grand Josun Busan.

blocks.text:
Professor Lee led “Understanding Design Intelligence” with Marília Biill, VP and Head of CMF Design at Kia, and Sujeong Choi, Senior Researcher. She also moderated
“Rediscovering the Everyday” with Yeontaek Lee, CEO of LG Electronics’ MyTasteCompany. FRAME is a culture and arts conference organised by Art Busan. Its first edition featured 10 sessions and 18 speakers across city, architecture, design, technology and lifestyle.

Running across both days, the Future Culture track explored new senses and forms of art shaped by technology, including AI, design intelligence and biomimicry. The first session looked at how lessons from nature can drive creative innovation. The second traced creative thinking from craft to future living. Around 200 participants joined FRAME 2025, which opened a new space for dialogue between the city and the arts. The sessions offered a chance to reflect on the role of design in connecting technology and everyday life.

title: Professor Cathy Lee Participates in Sustainability Panel at the 13th “From Lausanne to Beijing” International Fiber Art Biennale
lead: Professor Cathy Yeonchoo Lee of the International Design School for Advanced Studies (IDAS), Hongik University, participated as a panelist in the international academic forum of the 13th “From Lausanne to Beijing” International Fiber Art Biennale, held in Beijing on December 7, 2025.

blocks.text: The Biennale opened on December 6 at the Tsinghua University Art Museum under the theme “Interwoven Horizon.” This edition presents 205 works by 220 artists from 53 countries and regions. The exhibition runs through March 1, 2026, across five thematic sections at the Tsinghua University Art Museum, the Beijing Yingjie Museum of Stone Art, and the Today Art Museum.

The accompanying forum, “Interwoven Horizon: Fiber Art’s Response and Construction in the Intelligent Era,” examined artificial intelligence, ecological materials, the revival of craftsmanship, and cultural sustainability. Through cross-disciplinary dialogue, participants considered the theoretical and practical future of contemporary fiber art.

Professor Lee served on the afternoon panel, “The Texture of Sustainability: Natural Fibers and Future Lifestyles.” Fellow panelists included Gao Yang, Yuan Bo, and Wang Jian (China), Anett Papp (Hungary), and Kathrin Von Rechenberg (Germany). The discussion addressed the ecological ethics of cashmere in relation to regional culture and the emergence of a new naturalist lifestyle, tracing a shift from material ethics to design aesthetics.

Professor Chung Kyoung-Yeon, Dean of the Graduate School of Craft Arts at Hongik University, attended the opening ceremony. She also delivered a keynote address, “Reshaping Humanity,” during the morning session.

The Biennale reaffirmed fiber art as a critical medium for engaging with the complexities of the future, bringing craft, technology, and sustainability into international dialogue.

title: Designing the Boundary — Human Dignity That Design Must Uphold in an Era of Acceleration
lead: On May 9, the 2026 KICD Spring International Conference and International Invitational Exhibition was held at Gachon University under the theme "Borders," exploring the meaning of boundaries across design, culture, and society. Professor Cathy Lee of Hongik University IDAS delivered a keynote speech titled "Designing the Boundary," questioning what design must safeguard as technology penetrates deeper and faster into human life.

blocks.text: Background

blocks.caption:
2026 Keynote — Designing the Boundary
▲ Keynote Address by Professor Cathy Lee: "Designing the Boundary" — The Evolving Role of Design in Rapidly Changing Technological, Cultural, and Socioeconomic Contexts
blocks.text: Professor Cathy Lee opened her address by redefining design not as a matter of "what we make," but "what we decide." While design has always produced artifacts, she noted that the deeper inquiry lies in what design permits and what it refuses. Establishing boundaries, she emphasized, is not an act of limitation, but an act of "authorship"—declaring that certain values matter more than others and inscribing that conviction into the world.
Insight

blocks.caption:
Design as the Mediator — Between Technology and Human Dignity
▲ Design as a Mediator Between Technology and Human Dignity — Setting the Terms, Embodying Values, and Holding the Boundary
blocks.text: The core thesis of the speech was a clear declaration: "The challenge is no longer technological; it is directional." As AI becomes increasingly expansive, autonomous, and intimately woven into daily life, the essential question shifts from "what AI can do" to "what it should do, and from whose perspective." Design, she argued, is the very discipline that guards this boundary.

Traditionally, design has been understood as the creation of outputs and deliverables. Today, however, it is being repositioned as a critical discipline that shapes the human future, mediates complex systems, and defines the ethical frontiers of innovation. Professor Cathy Lee diagnosed our current reality as an "era of expanding capabilities," where AI and emerging technologies exhibit unprecedented expandability, autonomous judgment, and intimate closeness to human existence. Consequently, the center of gravity in design is shifting: from "Making Artifacts, Designing Products" to "Shaping the Future, Mediating Systems." The coordinates of design are moving from the hands that craft to the judgment that directs.

This philosophy translates into principles, and ultimately into real-world applications. Serving as a mediator between technology and human dignity, design must set the terms, embody values, and hold the boundary. The constant question to ask is: "Does this affirm human life, or does it merely optimize it?" Citing the "Designed with Human Dignity" project conducted in collaboration with Hyundai Motor Group, she illustrated how principles of Respect, Care, Co-Existence, and Trust are implemented within industrial frameworks. In closing, she emphasized a "mindset" that transcends methodology. While tools can be transferred and methods can be taught, navigating a world that struggles even to name its own crises demands more than a toolkit. Mindset is more than an attitude—it is the catalyst for transforming the world, bridging generations, and opening new pathways for leadership.

title: Human Factors in Leadership (DEIA & Design) Workshop Held at Hongik University
lead: The international design workshop “Human Factors in Leadership (DEIA & Design)” took place from December 9 to 12, 2024, at Yemungwan Hall, Hongik University. The program aimed to develop future leaders by combining design leadership with a global mindset.

blocks.text:
The workshop integrated DEIA (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, Accessibility) values into design. It offered a platform for inclusive design practice and stronger strategic thinking. Participants included Hongik University students in emerging technology design and students from the International Design School for Advanced Studies (IDAS).

Two facilitators led the program. Enrique Martinez is a professor at the Federal Executive Institute, part of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM), and an expert in government design leadership. Professor Cathy Yeonchoo Lee teaches Design Management at IDAS.

Over four days, the facilitators examined how design leadership shapes corporate strategy and government policy. They presented a range of problem-solving strategies and innovative approaches. Participants explored DEIA-centered design thinking and practice, building strategic skills and a broader global perspective.

The program also included a dialogue with UNDP (United Nations Development Programme). The discussion covered DEI-driven business strategy and directions for policy research. UNDP works in around 170 countries to end poverty, reduce inequality and support sustainable development.

The workshop offered a space to explore how inclusive values can shape design leadership across business and public policy. More programs are planned to develop creative leadership and global design talent.

title: International Design Workshop “Apart — Together” Held at Hongik University with UNDP
lead: The International Design School for Advanced Studies (IDAS), Hongik University, and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) hosted the international design workshop “Apart — Together” on November 13 and 14, 2025, at Yemungwan Hall. Under the theme “Design Between the Individual and the Collective,” the two-day program examined how individual action can drive collective change.

blocks.text: The workshop was led by two facilitators. Enrique Martinez is a Design, Innovation and Strategy Advisor and a faculty member of the Federal Executive Institute, part of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Soren Vester Haldrup is a Policy Advisor at the UNDP Global Policy Centre for Governance, with a focus on applying design thinking to complex public-sector systems.

On the first day, participants mapped their personal histories onto a timeline. They then set these against major global and national events of the same period, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, reflecting on how larger shifts had shaped their own lives.

The program also introduced how UNDP applies design in its work. Through short lectures, discussions, and hands-on making activities, participants considered the kind of designer and agent of change they aspire to be, both as individuals and as members of a wider community.

At the conclusion of the program, each participant pitched an original idea. These proposals were brought together in a Collective Impact Map, connecting individual perspectives into a shared framework for action.

The workshop underscored the role of design in bridging individual agency and collective impact across public and global contexts.

title: Professor Cathy Lee Moderates Global Mindset Session at FRAME 2026
lead:
Professor Cathy Lee of Hongik University’s International Design School for Advanced
Studies (IDAS) moderated the “Global Mindset” session on 9 October, the first day of
FRAME 2026 at Nurimaru APEC House in Busan.

blocks.text:
Professor Lee led a conversation with Simon Loasby, Head of Hyundai Design Center, and Betty J. Chung, Professor and Academic Director of Korea University Global MBA.
FRAME is a global art and culture conference hosted by Busan Metropolitan City and organised by Art Busan. Now in its second year, it ran over two days and featured 16 leaders
from eight fields across six sessions.

This year’s theme was “People Who Stand by Their Convictions.” The session explored how leaders navigate diverse cultures and markets while staying true to their own philosophy and identity. It also examined how cultural perspectives can become a foundation for sustainable business and lasting value.

Both days of FRAME 2026 sold out, drawing around 250 participants. Around 70 percent were in their 20s and 30s. The session offered a space to explore what global design leadership means where design, business and culture meet.
